projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Watson Warriner was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Interviewer
sp.p: The -- see, Dad -- Dad, when he came back from the war, he worked -- he worked at Seaford for DuPont.

sp.speaker: Watson Warriner
sp.p: Oh, he did?

sp.speaker: Unidentified Interviewer
sp.p: Yeah. He didn't want to go back to Johnny -- he didn't want to go back to his family -- the family business. He wanted to stay in DuPont Engineering.

sp.speaker: Watson Warriner
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Interviewer
sp.p: So he was down in Seaford for, I think, the first year after he got back.

sp.speaker: Watson Warriner
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Interviewer
sp.p: So --

sp.speaker: Watson Warriner
sp.p: Well, he -- Jim Reed knew John quite well.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Interviewer
sp.p: Oh, yeah. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Watson Warriner
sp.p: And Granville Read -- of course chief engineer. Granville hired me as a young engineer. So at that particular meeting, Jim was there, and there was -- and maybe --

sp.speaker: Unidentified Speaker
sp.p: Okay. Got it.

sp.speaker: Watson Warriner
sp.p: -- maybe John, your dad at that time, was working for DuPont, but I don't think so.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Interviewer
sp.p: But see, he was -- well, no. He went -- they graduate -- let's see. The war started in '41, right?

sp.speaker: Watson Warriner
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Interviewer
sp.p: September 7, 1941.

sp.speaker: Watson Warriner
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Interviewer
sp.p: I don't think he -- he graduated from Delaware in like '39 maybe.

sp.speaker: Watson Warriner
sp.p: You know, what -- what might have happened -- let's back up a little bit. I was up here working on the, you know, the atomic bomb --

sp.speaker: Unidentified Interviewer
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Watson Warriner
sp.p: -- in 1943. (Break in video)

sp.speaker: Watson Warriner
sp.p: My name is Watson Warriner. And I was born and raised in Richmond, Virginia. And I attended Virginia Polytechnic Institute, which is known as Virginia Tech. And I graduated there in 1938 with a BS degree in chemical engineering. The Depression was on, and jobs were very hard to find, but believe it, DuPont did finally hire me in February 1939 in the engineering department. So I went to work for DuPont here in Wilmington, but I went to work over -- I was actually working at the chambers works, but I was a part of the engineering department. Wonderful place to work. We made everything there: tetraethyl lead, alcohol, synthetic rubber, which is neoprene. I worked in a neoprene plant. Everything was going along fine. 1940 comes along. War clouds are gathering very seriously. And the British and French Purchasing Commission has prevailed on the government to build a powder plant for them, a gunpowder plant, on the -- for them. DuPont was asked to do this. And so right away, DuPont accepted the job, and it's going to turn out to be the Tennessee Powder Company, going to be built 25 miles north of Memphis, Tennessee. And so they grabbed up about five of us young engineers. I'm chemical. The others were either chemical or mechanical. They weren't civil. And they put us into the construction division, transferred us to Memphis in the construction division, June of 1940. And they put us in positions, assistant division engineers, assistants to seasoned construction men. I ended up being assistant division engineer in the acid area, and this is an area that takes ammonia and converts it to nitric acid by the oxidation of ammonia. And then we concentrate that acid from 62 percent nitrate to 90 percent. And that is what they used to nitrate what was cotton linters, spelled L-I-N-T-E-R-S, little short fibers of cotton. And you -- that is what gunpowder consists of. And it's gunpowder for big cannons and rifles and that type of thing. Also at that plant, we -- they had put in two lines of TNT, which also requires nitric acid because it's trinitrotoluene.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Interviewer
sp.p: Now let me ask you something.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Speaker
sp.p: TJ, can we -- a little closer to the camera, please. Just a little more access here.

sp.speaker: Watson Warriner
sp.p: How does it come across? Okay?

sp.speaker: Unidentified Speaker
sp.p: Excellent.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Interviewer
sp.p: Right here? Am I good?

sp.speaker: Unidentified Speaker
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Interviewer
sp.p: Right here?

sp.speaker: Unidentified Speaker
sp.p: Thanks. Yeah. Right there. Just keep looking at TJ.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Interviewer
sp.p: Tell me what -- what was the separation between Hercules then and DuPont? Wasn't Hercules the big dynamite company?

sp.speaker: Watson Warriner
sp.p: Hercules -- DuPont came under the Sherman Antitrust Law, which I believe was in 1912, and was broken up into Hercules and Atlas Powder and DuPont. So that's the way Atlas came about -- I mean Hercules came about. It was about -- when they did the breakup, I think it was about half the size of -- of DuPont. And Atlas was about half the size of Hercules. This is during the breakup period.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Interviewer
sp.p: Now, did -- did they -- did they sort of work out of a combined -- that's what I was getting to. When you made this factory, was it just DuPont product they were making, or were they also making Hercules products and Atlas products?

sp.speaker: Watson Warriner
sp.p: Was this -- the gunpowder we were making was for all military -- what we call military explosives. And what we were doing, we -- the companies were entirely separated, back years before I started to work for them. As a matter of fact, controlled by law that DuPont could not have anything to do with Hercules and vice versa. So everything that we manufactured -- we've gone now -- we're embarking now -- let me get back to my original story. The -- we started work then June. It turned out to be really a small Manhattan Project because it was dire need to get this material. DuPont -- the U.S. government did not -- did not have very much military explosive. And so we got everything we needed to do on this plant. It was a 30 million dollar plant, which was a lot of money in 1940s. And of course the Depression was still on. We had no problem in getting good men to build this plant. This is June 1940 when we were driving concrete piles to erect a powerhouse, which we generated our own electricity. And by December, we had this plant up and were nitrating cotton linters in December. In six months, we were producing powder. The thing of it, in September of 1940, France fell. They capitulated to the Germans. So the British and French Purchase Commission no longer existed. United States took this over on what they call a lend-lease. That was the beginning of lend-lease. And they changed it -- changed the name to the Chickasaw ordnance works. And from then on, it operated. It was a government- owned plant. DuPont just designed, built it and operated it for the U.S. government, like they did -- every ensuing plant I'm going to talk about did the same way, including the big Manhattan district. It was all done, designed, built and operated by DuPont. And for 1 dollar. The contract for doing this was 1 dollar for each one of these plants, which over the period of time we're talking about here, from 1940 through 1944, you're talking -- I don't know -- a dozen and a half plants, at least.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Interviewer
sp.p: They did that for 1 dollar?

sp.speaker: Watson Warriner
sp.p: They got -- they got a dollar.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Interviewer
sp.p: For each plant or for --

sp.speaker: Watson Warriner
sp.p: Each plant, they got a dollar.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Interviewer
sp.p: Okay. So -- so the way this worked was DuPont didn't really manufacture product. The government manufactured their own product under -- under your guidelines? No.

sp.speaker: Watson Warriner
sp.p: The plant was designed, built and operated completely by DuPont people.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Interviewer
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Watson Warriner
sp.p: The government was done -- being done by the government. There were government people located on the plant, but they had little to do with the design, construction and operation of the plant. This was 99.9 percent DuPont. And we maintained that all through the war.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Interviewer
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Watson Warriner
sp.p: Because they -- the government by that time knew DuPont was very, very expert at what they did, and so we -- we had a free rein to do what we did or do what we had to do, and we did it. So I went from Mem -- we completed that job in -- at the end of 1940. Now the war has gotten very bad. I mean, the war clouds are terrible. And so now our construction division is being split up into kind of two -- two bunches. The crowd that I was going to be with, we went to the Alabama, went down to Childersburg, Alabama, about 50 miles south of Birmingham to build the Alabama ordnance works in a -- nothing but a big red clay cornfield. By the end -- and here again, we were going to have a smokeless powder plant like we did in Memphis and also some TNT lines, trinitrotoluene, for bombs. And we got under way with that and -- by January of '41, and we completed that by the end of the year. It was all up and running and producing. Then got transferred from there up to the Wabash River ordnance works. A beautiful cornfield on condemned farm -- farmland. And here, we're going to have a nitric acid plant, like we have at every one of these sites because you need nitric acid at all of them. So at the Wabash River ordnance works, which is --

sp.speaker: Unidentified Interviewer
sp.p: Where was that --

sp.speaker: Watson Warriner
sp.p: 25 miles north of Terre Haute in a place called Newport, Indiana, on the Wabash River -- on the Wabash River, because they need river water to keep everything cool. And now we have to have a nitric acid plant, which I was the division engineer in charge of erection of this big nitric acid plant and the concentration of the acid. And now we're going to nitrate hexamine. And we're going to produce -- commercially produce plastic explosive for the first time in the world. And this is a awful material that terrorists today use, but this is why we did it. Nitrating hexamine. I was in charge of the acid area there. And then the plant went into production about September of forty -- 1941 -- '2. 1942. And they transferred me out of construction to be -- unbelievable at this young age -- I was called chief engineer in charge of operating maintenance. That -- I was in charge of maintenance for the acid plant and the two nitrating lines where we actually took the acid and nitrated the hexamine to make material we called RDX, but I think today in some -- in some cases it's called C4, but it is plastic explosive. And we -- the Allies really wanted -- we really wanted this material because it turned out very well to be used in what we call blockbuster bombs. And so that was the beginning of that. I was in this job of chief engineer of maintenance there. I'd been in that job for about four months. In January of 1943, I got summonsed up to the plant manager's office on a Monday morning. And he handed me a telegram. And I said -- his name happened to be Walter O. Simon, S-I-M-O-N. He was the plant manager there. And as the story will end in a little while, he is going to end up being the plant manager of the Hanford engineer works, which is a plant, the giant plant that we -- I'm going to talk about this later. But anyway, Walter Simon, Walt Simon handed me this telegram. It was from E.G. Atgutt, and it said Watson Warriner is to report to the engineering department at once. And I said, "Walter, what's this?" He said, "Watson, I don't know. We've been informed by the Wilmington management that a big project, secret project, is under way, and if personnel is requested through normal channels, the person is to be made available at once. So here it is. And your job is over here. Get out of here tomorrow." Now, here it is in late January. Snow on the ground. Ice on the ground.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Interviewer
sp.p: Were you married yet?

sp.speaker: Watson Warriner
sp.p: I was not married. I did not get married until 1945. So I'm a bachelor. No problem. You could pack up and move in a hurry. I had a 1940 Ford convertible coupe, which I'd bought in Memphis. I paid 1100 dollars for this. The most expensive car that Ford produced at that time. It's -- a sedan, four-door sedan cost 750 dollar. So I had this convertible coupe. It had a heater, a radio and an automatic top and horse -- horse leather for seats. It was a jump seat. So anyway, how can I -- I said, well, how can I drive this to Wilmington? I mean, there's snow and ice on the ground. I've got to go up through Pittsburgh and everything. There was no interstates or nothing. Nobody salted any roads in those days. So he calls in the transportation department, manager of the transportation department. He said, "Look. Watson is to be on the Spirit of St. Louis tomorrow." It's a fast train on the Pennsylvania Railroad from St. Louis to Philadelphia, all-Pullman train. "And you put his car on the freight train and ship it to Wilmington." So that's what they did. So I showed up in Wilmington. And this was late January, right around February the 1st. And we -- we -- the engineering department, which I had been a member of before. So we entered, this group of us entered the room, and they gradually began to tell us what -- what we were going to do. And the first thing is it's going to be a highly confidential secret job and that we were going to be given a Q clearance. And we -- in order to have a Q clearance -- we needed that because we will need to know things about this project that will be denied other people. So they clearly made this very clear to us. They read us -- I be -- it was a statement. I believe it was the Espionage Act of 1938 or something like that. It was a law. And they read this to us. You had to read it yourself. They had witnesses there to see that you read this. And then you signed a statement that you fully understood this and that you would abide by this. And it was witnessed by -- these are all DuPont people, witnessed by -- that. So now you are under sworn testimony here that you are not going to reveal to anyone information that you are made privy to on this project.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Interviewer
sp.p: Did they -- did they -- did they have background checks in those days?

sp.speaker: Unidentified Speaker
sp.p: Just adjust something. Just a short second.

sp.speaker: Watson Warriner
sp.p: My -- my -- my family in Richard, Virginia had told me on several occasions that the neighbors and people that I'd worked for in summertime, the government had -- government agents had been there checking on me. So we --

sp.speaker: Unidentified Interviewer
sp.p: And then you graduated from Virginia Tech, right?

sp.speaker: Watson Warriner
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Interviewer
sp.p: How did they ever -- I didn't think anybody from Virginia Tech could ever get a secret clearance for anything.

sp.speaker: Watson Warriner
sp.p: (laughter) Well, maybe not. But anyway -- but -- So what -- this is the way we -- we entered the -- this group. And there was four or five or six of them in my particular group. I knew these fellows from past jobs we'd been on. And they are now going to distribute us into the design division of the DuPont engineering department, which is located on the 13th floor of the Nemours building, which the company even no longer owns. It became known around as Shangri-la because no one was permitted to enter that area. This is where all the confidential drawing -- the drawing rooms are there. All confidential. It was under surveillance all the time. And as a matter of fact, even on the 13th floor of the DuPont building, they came around and sealed the locks on every window, even though it was on the -- and during the day, several times a day -- I was working in the office there, on this project -- these guards would come around and check the seals. These are the window seals on the lock -- on the 13th floor. And to make sure that nobody was entering or leaving this area, even on the 13th floor window. So getting back to the clearance thing again, the only two people that -- the only people I know that died on account of revealing stuff on the bomb were the Rosenbergs, who were -- worked at Los Alamos and made information on the bomb design to Canadian spies, which ended up in foreign hands and caused -- Mr. and Mrs. Rosenberg unfortunately were elect -- put to death for that revelation. Now, this is what we knew -- this happened long after we had signed this, but they had signed the same piece of paper, and that's what happened to them. So it was a well-guarded secret. And so right away, they put me into the design division. And I started work under -- under senior engineers. I was a young engineer and under senior engineers. And the first thing they wanted -- we were to do was we're going to design three heavy water plants. And you do this by -- Heavy water occurs in nature. I think it's 1 part in every 16,000 parts of water is heavy water. You've been drinking heavy water all your life. It's just the way it occurs in nature, that way. And what you do is you -- you -- you just distill steam and separate it. That's the way we did it, fractionating steam. The plants were -- that we had -- that we built were just a series of big tall columns, looked like an oil refinery except that the first -- the first column we put up was a field erected 15 feet in diameter. And it went a hundred feet high with bubble trays and everything inside of it. And the next one down in size, what came out of the top of that went into the bottom of the next one. As I recall, it was 12'6". And then from then on, the columns could all be fabricated on plan and shipped in by train. You might have to put them on a couple of flatcars to get them in. But we built -- they were designed and built and operated; one was in Morgantown, West Virginia, which was the site of a government ammonia plant, which we built for the government. And the second one was twice as big as the first one, and that was going into the Alabama ordnance works in Childersburg, Alabama, which I was -- had worked on in 1941. And the third one was going into the Wabash River ordnance works. It was going to be three times bigger than the first one. And that was the plant that I worked in in 1943. So we got these up. As we were designing these -- and one of the reasons we thought the government was looking at heavy water, and that is one way to moderate neutrons in nuclear power. And one of the thoughts was that Germany had invaded Norway to get a heavy water plant because Norway had a heavy water plant that they made by the electrolysis -- the electrolysis of water is how they did theirs. A lot of electricity always. So while we were working on this, the commandos, the British commandos, I believe helped by the Canadian, the Canadian commandos, went into that plant, sneaked into that plant at nighttime and destroyed a good part of it. In other words, it was to sabotage the plant. Well, next morning on the radio and on the paper, they told us all about this. Well, we got up and sort of danced around in the office because this was going to help us get ahead of the Germans. And so we -- this point, I'd finished that. With good senior engineers, I'm working on it. And then they transferred me to what they called a separations area. Now we're going to work on taking the slugs from the -- uranium slugs, which have been irradiated in the piles; reacted to, want to call them. Also known as piles. And we were going to take these irradiated slugs, and they were coming over -- over to the separations area. And that's where we separate, get the plutonium out of the 30-plus other radioactive materials that have been created from this uranium. And those other 30 radioactive materials is going to be waste, and that is the current waste that is a terrible problem at the plant at -- at Man -- at the Manhattan Project plant in Hanford, Washington today. There's an enormous project there now which is going to concentrate that waste from over 100 underground tanks -- tanks of 750,000 gallons each, concrete enclosed. And the plan is under way at the Hanford engineer works today to glassify that, pump it out, concentrate it, enclose it in glass, glassify it. Then enclose that glassed cylinder into a stainless cylinder, and it would be heading to Yucca Flats, Nevada, if you can ever get Nevada pleased enough with accepting. But that's all designed to be headed that way. And this -- this is going on now. It will be going on for the next 10 years. So anyway, I'm in the -- now in the separations area, and it's my job that -- to work with these senior engineers. We're designing the equipment that's going to be used to do the separation. It was a water process. And what you do is you precipitate and then centrifuge. We had big solid bowl centrifuges, as I recall them, in one of these separations buildings of 40 cells each. Each cell contained within a building. These are cells within the building. Each one of these would contain a tank and a centrifuge. Centrifuges were -- would have a -- it was a solid bowl centrifuge, just like a washing machine, only the bowl was solid. And it would have a 30-horsepower motor on it to turn it. All this -- as I recall, we had 11-step centrifuging and precipitating steps in each 221 building, and we had three of these buildings. And so the first -- the first step that -- these slugs would come over in what we called a cast car. It was a big, lead cast, mounted armor, railroad flatcar. And it would leave the reactor area. First thing it would do from the reactors, they would push this -- get these slugs out of the pile and push them into stainless steel buckets. And these buckets would then be cooled for 30 days in a reservoir, on the water reservoir. All this had to be done remotely, too, because it was hot. Then they would take these stainless steel containers full of slugs, uranium slugs, which are enclosed in an aluminum enclosure. And these would come over to the 200 area in a cast car, railroad cast car. We would have two or three flatcars between the cast car and the locomotive. And he would come across the desert 3 or 4 miles to get from a reactor plant to the 221. The 221 building, we had three of those. He would go along, you know, 5 or 10 miles an hour, but in case he had a derailment. And a lid of the big, lead cast -- the cast had tens of -- over 10 inches of lead, thick walls. If they ever had a derailment and he spilled these things out, at least the engineer would be two or three car lengths away. Obviously at 10 or 15 miles an hour, you're not likely to have a derailment, and I don't think they ever did. These would come over to the 221 building. And he would back this car into the 221 building, which now -- 221 building, 800 feet long. You have 40 cells in there. You have an overhead crane traveling the entire distance here. And he's going to unload these. He's going to drop the car in this place, and they're going to close the canyon door, and then a crane will come along, overhead crane come along, lift the lid off of the cast car and take these vessels, these stainless steel cans, if you want to call them, full of slugs and unload them. Then the first step you would have in the 221 building is you would remotely -- this is all done remotely. They'd take this can -- one of these can fulls of things, about the size of a garbage can, but all made out of 25/12 Cb -- not 18/8 Cb, but 25/12 Cb. And they're going to be processed. And equipment all the way through this canyon, everything is 25/12 Cb. All the pipe, tanks, centrifuges, all -- not 18/8, but 25/12. And so the -- these cans would be upended into the first step, which was called a dissolver. And then from -- we'd dissolve off -- we'd dissolve the aluminum can or the enclosure off. And that would go to the waste tanks. And now the -- you have aluminum. Process of dissolving and precipitating, centrifuging and repeating that, I think is 11 times in a 221 building. You finally get down to the point where you have pretty -- pretty good plutonium. I mean pretty pure plutonium. And what we did, we would end up with plutonium nitrate. It was, at the end, a very, very syrupy, thick somewhat, solution. And that is what got shipped to Los Alamos to -- and when they got it, they would -- they would reduce it to plutonium metal and create a bomb from it. So now getting back to --

sp.speaker: Unidentified Interviewer
sp.p: Did you know what the end result was going to be?

sp.speaker: Watson Warriner
sp.p: We -- we knew it was going to be a bomb. We had some reason to believe that Los Alamos had something to do with this, but -- because we had people that would visit Los Alamos. Now, they would not come back and tell us what they were doing, but we -- we -- we were almost sure that a bomb is going to be the result of what we were doing. The fact that Los Alamos actually did the bomb, I was never aware of that, but I knew they had something -- something to do with the project. But get back to the 221 building, the overhead crane we had, as I recall, was made by Whiting, W-H-I-T-I-N-G, and it ran the entire length of the canyon over these 40 cells. And the cab of the crane was behind a -- a concrete wall. Obviously the concrete wall could cover -- the cab attendant would be overhung behind this wall. The wall ran the entire existence of the canyon. And the cab was coated, was encased in lead. In other words, we had heavy lead outside of all this. So the penetration of radioactive from the canyon could not get to the operator in the -- in the cab of this crane. The crane is the nerve center and everything of this entire building. If anything happens to that crane, you're not going to process anything because the minute you introduce radioactive stuff into the dissolver and get on with the process, the canyon becomes radioactively hot and is inaccessible by man. So here we have the Whiting crane. And underneath the two crane beams, spanning the canyon, there are two submarine-type telescopes. These telescopes are connected electrically. I believe they called it a selsyn, S-E-L-S-Y-N, electrical connection, so they ran -- always ran together. And they could run back and forth across the canyon. The eyepieces were in the cab. He could rotate the -- the -- the eyepieces on the other end, the telescoped end, over the canyon so that he had depth perception because we had a telescope on the -- on the -- under the beam, two beams that make -- make the crane -- that the crane is constructed from. So now he can look down into the canyon 40 feet below and see everything that he has to do. Now, on one cable is a -- an electrically operated impact wrench. And that wrench will fit over the hexagon- type stud of what we called a pipe connector. We called them jumpers because we had pipe jumpers for conducting liquids from tank to tank and from cell to cell. And we also had electrical jumpers because we had electrical motors, as I mentioned before, 30-horsepower centrifuge motor. And these -- we had -- in order to maintain maintenance in this place, if anything went wrong, it would take -- they used a crane, and we had -- with the impact wrench, they were able to unloose all the connectors, electrical and piping, lay it in beside. They could remove the tank, take it down to Cell -- I think -- there were 40 cells in here, and I think 37 -- 37, 38 and 39 or 40, they would called junk cells. And if you had bad equipment or something sprung a leak, you couldn't take this out and throw it in the backyard. You'd take it to one of these junk cells and put it in there. And then you would come through -- through another what we called a mockup building, and we had mockup cell in that building which exactly duplicated the cell outline and pipe connections and electrical connections that we had in the canyon. And you would put a new tank or new centrifuge, go through the mockup building with all the connectors, and then you would move that just like -- with a crane into the tunnel of the 221 building, and just like you unloaded the -- the containers of slugs, you would unload the tank, the jumpers. And with the overhead crane, with the -- with the telescope and the impact wrench, you would install these, all remotely, and you would get the thing back into operation. Because you could not go into the canyon with a man to do this.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Interviewer
sp.p: How -- if you couldn't do that, I mean how long would it take to clear the canyon out? Did you ever clear it out?

sp.speaker: Watson Warriner
sp.p: Never. I don't think you could ever clear it out.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Interviewer
sp.p: You mean to this day, basically?

sp.speaker: Watson Warriner
sp.p: In other words, if anything happened to that -- that crane, the canyon would be dead. And what happened, we had the crane -- when -- we worked with the crane manufacturer on this. And the main cables, we had installed under the -- when they came off the drum, that was a big, hydraulic, knife device that if you were -- had the crane doing some of this work down in the canyon, and some way, somehow the hook got hung up on something, and you could not move the crane, this building would be out of service. So through this hydraulic knife, you could cut the cable remotely from the cab, and at least that would release the crane. And he could come down to the unloading area where we unloaded the slugs and close a door, that big, big, vertical closing door. And there, maintenance people could go in and put a new cable and hook on that.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Interviewer
sp.p: Oh, okay. So you could --

sp.speaker: Watson Warriner
sp.p: Whether that -- whether that ever had to be done or not, I don't know, but --

sp.speaker: Unidentified Interviewer
sp.p: So you could dec -- you could decontaminate the crane? I mean when you moved it into the other building and shut the door for the canyon.

sp.speaker: Watson Warriner
sp.p: At least what you could do is -- you -- I'm sure they could try to decontaminate it, but one thing you can do in there, you can have limited access of human beings. In other words, a human being can stand so much radiation, but you won't give him too much. So by the rotation of a number of people, you could go in and make the necessary repairs.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Interviewer
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Watson Warriner
sp.p: Whether they ever had to do that or not, I'm not -- I don't -- I'm not aware of them having to do that ever, but the facility was there for doing it. None of these facilities are working anymore anyhow. The plant is completely shut down.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Interviewer
sp.p: Oh, it is.

sp.speaker: Watson Warriner
sp.p: Yes. The only thing that they're doing at the Hanford engineer works today is working on the disposal of the waste. And the 105-B reactor, which is the one that went into production first, it is on the verge of becoming a national monument. Whether they will ever make a national monument out of the separation area is not known at the present time.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Interviewer
sp.p: Have you been back out there?

sp.speaker: Watson Warriner
sp.p: I've been out there -- I was a guest of Westinghouse -- GE. I mean -- let's go back to DuPont. DuPont vacated this place in -- I think it was August of 1946. It was the latter part of 1946. And DuPont, who said at the very beginning they did not want to keep on operating this plant, they got out of it there and turned it over to GE. I think it was in August of 1946. Thereabouts. And so -- and then ultimately, I think GE got out of it. In 1996, Westinghouse was in charge. And I think they're now beginning to think about what they're going to do with all of this waste. So I spent a day as a guest of Westinghouse. I was not -- I instituted this visit, but they were polite enough to give me a guide and recognized the fact that I had been there. I had my identification, so forth and so on. And out of politeness to that, they gave me a guide. I had him all day. Took me over the entire project, and -- which I enjoyed. I am going back on October the 15th. They have a road tour of the entire project. It lasts four hours, and I'm going to be there and go to that. I plan to take my hardhat with me, and I'm -- want to hand me my hardhat? Doing okay?

sp.speaker: Unidentified Interviewer
sp.p: Well, I'm going to put that -- see if you can -- here. See if you can go in --

sp.speaker: Unidentified Speaker
sp.p: Good. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Interviewer
sp.p: He's going to told up his -- hold up your badge like that or like this. Take it with the one, like that. You can just look at me. He's going to pan in on you. Look at me. TJ. Okay.

sp.speaker: Watson Warriner
sp.p: Did you get it?

sp.speaker: Unidentified Interviewer
sp.p: Yeah. Hat off there.

sp.speaker: Watson Warriner
sp.p: Still got more time. You want to --

sp.speaker: Unidentified Interviewer
sp.p: -- do that.

sp.speaker: Watson Warriner
sp.p: Oh. (laughter)

sp.speaker: Unidentified Interviewer
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Watson Warriner
sp.p: Yes. Ready to start again?

sp.speaker: Unidentified Interviewer
sp.p: Let's see. We're going to do -- what do we want to talk about now?

sp.speaker: Watson Warriner
sp.p: John asked them -- some statistics here that are very interesting on this plant.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Interviewer
sp.p: Okay. Okay. All right. You ready? Go ahead.

sp.speaker: Watson Warriner
sp.p: Okay. Well, this project that we had, the Manhattan Project -- you want to show my certificates in -- in --

sp.speaker: Unidentified Interviewer
sp.p: I'm going to copy those.

sp.speaker: Watson Warriner
sp.p: Okay. This was a massive project, the Manhattan Project. And some of the statistics that we had -- we created a village there, which is the third largest city in -- in the state of Washington. And it was called -- the name of it was Hanford. It was a construction camp. It was a bunch of igloos, quonset huts. We had hospitals, drugstores, conf -- it was a city. Barbershops, everything. We had 35,000 men working there at its peak. And in order to get these men out to the outlying areas -- after all, this site is a third the size of Delaware. It was 600 square miles. Delaware is 1800 square miles. It's 600 square miles. And we -- the manufacturing facilities, three reactors: B, D and F. And two -- three big separations buildings, which was T, U, B and C, except we cancelled C. Didn't build C. Because we only needed three separation buildings to go with the three reactors. They were widely separated because if you had a nuclear accident in one of the buildings, they did not want to have to shut down the other ones. So in order to get the men out and to work in these outlying areas, we had over 800 buses that they ran. It was the largest bus system in the world. It -- the biggest bus system in the world at that time was Chicago, and we had more buses than the city of Chicago did. There was a hundred -- there was 158 miles of -- yeah. 158 miles of railroad track within this site, because we're moving stuff, but particularly going from the reactors to the separations buildings, all going to be done by railcars. And we had -- we unloaded 40,000 carloads of material to build this plant. We had 780,000 cubic yards of concrete on this plant. And the big separations buildings that we were talking about used the most concrete for any single building out there. And they had, each one, about 85,000 yards of concrete in each 221 separations building. We had 8500 pieces of construction equipment there, cranes, bulldozers. And you name it, we had it. 8500 pieces. We moved 25 million cubic yards of earth there to build the plant. And so that gives you some idea of what we -- what we had there. All created and done from the time the experiment was under the stadium, done by Enrico Fermi in the Chicago -- the other Chicago stadium. I think it was September of 1942. He demonstrated in a carbon-moderated pile that you could take uranium and make plutonium, convert it to plutonium. Make Element 92 and end up with Element 94. The plutonium he made is the most -- the only plutonium that existed in the world at that time. And he made 1 milligram. Well, 1 milligram is -- you know, is 454 grams per pound. And so at 45,400 milligrams in a pound of material. Now, that's all they had. Now they come to DuPont and said, "You've got -- we know the Germans are ahead of us, and if they get the bomb before we do, we'll all end up speaking German." And so this is in September 1940 -- 1942. And DuPont right away jumps on this job to do it because the government says, "We believe you're the only company that can do this." And DuPont said, "Well, if anybody can do it, we can." And they accepted the job. And that was right away, in January of 1943. And I started work on it in February of '43, so that's what happened. So from the time they had the experiment on the stadium until the bomb was dropped on August the 6th, it was exactly 32 months. Now, how on earth was something like this possible? We had no cell phones. We had no radios. We did not have any tel -- you know, telephone walkie-talkies. We didn't have any walkie-talkies. All we had was slide rules, manual calculators. And we did have ditto machines. And -- and it was all done. And -- and everything worked. I mean, can you imagine from the start to finish of a job of this magnitude, what could go wrong? Nothing went wrong. As a matter of fact, I -- on a side trip, I got sent to DuPont, Washington because they wanted somebody that knew how to put the nitric acid plant together. And it was a tiny little part of the Manhattan Project, only it was located in the company plant in DuPont, Washington, dynamite plant. While I was there -- and we did get that plant all put up and as it was going to be shipped. The destination of the acid was secret. Making nitric acid is not secret, but the destination was. I knew where it was going, but nobody else did. It was Hanford. And that would be -- that nitric acid would be used in the dissolver to dissolve the can that I mentioned earlier in the program, the can surrounding the uranium slug. And it was used in the final step in the 221 buildings to convert the plutonium to plutonium nitrate. It's a syrupy solution that's going to Los Alamos. While I was there at DuPont, Washington, just a few miles south of Tacoma, I witnessed a huge airplane coming over. We all looked at it. This plane would come over, and it would circle around. And you could kind of tell that they were trying to -- you know, flying the plane to see how it behaved. And it was the biggest thing you've ever seen. It was much -- it was not a B-17. It turned out to be the B-29, which they were building in the state of Washington, by Boeing. And so -- but -- so the B-29 came along just in time for it to be modified into accommodating not only Little Boy, but mainly Fat Man. Fat Man was the plutonium bomb. And then we had no satellites, no weather satellites to show us the proper days and everything to take this bomb. We had none of that. So the only thing that I can conclude, and I think -- I don't think I'm alone in this. The United States, being the great nation we are -- it's a dignified nation. We base everything here on the desire for mankind. We had our backs against the wall, against two vicious empires. The Germans were putting 6 million Jews to death. The Japanese had invaded the Philippines and bayoneted people in hospitals and -- and actually taken babies and pinned them on the end of the bayonets into the wall and the rape of Nanking. So this is what we were up against, terrible people. So if you ask me, I think somebody helped us out with this. And I'll just have to leave it up to you. I just know that somebody helped us with this. And in order to conclude the program, today the United States is faced with the same thing. We have a terrible bunch of enemies here. And some way, somehow, I hope that -- I know we'll survive, but I certainly hope that the same help that we got from this unknown power will guide us and help us defeat the terrible enemy we have today.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Interviewer
sp.p: Did -- when you talked about under the stadium, tell me about under the stadium, what that means.

sp.speaker: Watson Warriner
sp.p: The enemy -- Enrico Fermi, who was a Italian, world- class Italian physicist, he --

sp.speaker: Unidentified Interviewer
sp.p: And how did he get here? Was he brought back over here to us? Or did he -- did he jump ship over there, or was he from --

sp.speaker: Watson Warriner
sp.p: Well, I think he came over in the normal way.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Interviewer
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Watson Warriner
sp.p: I mean, Einstein -- Einstein, who was also in on the bomb, Einstein proved mathematically that you could make a bomb. E is equal to mc2 is what -- what Einstein proved mathematically could be done. And that is exactly what you see when the bomb goes off. The energy that you're looking at is taking a small amount of material; in the case of -- in the case of the Hiroshima bomb, it was 45 pounds, as I recall, of U-235. And in the Nagasaki bomb, I think it was about 14 and a half pounds of plutonium. And E is equal to mc2. E is energy that you're seeing, which is light and heat. And m is the mass that you are converting -- you're totally converting that mass that I just told you about, completely converted that to light and heat. And then c is the constant, which happens to be the speed of light. So you can see -- if you take the speed of light, which is 186,000 miles a second, and you square that, you can see what an enormous amount of E you have. E is a big number. So the reason he was -- he did this under the stadium, as you asked, was he was going to take carbon blocks. Now, he used carbon blocks -- and carbon is used to slow the neutrons down. It's called a moderator, a neutron moderator. And you need to slow them in aiding neutrons coming from the radio -- some native radioactivity within the uranium. But the neutrons are firing at speed of light 186,000 miles a second. They're very, very small, very -- almost weightless. So they will just keep on shooting back and forth through the reactor. But you want to slow them down, so they will be drawn into the center of an atom. And that's why the neutron split the atom. And that's why the -- why you make the conversions from one material to another. So -- and that's what heavy water also does. It is a neutron moderator, which now is used in nuclear reactors. All -- they don't want carbon anymore. As a matter of fact, the bad accident they had in Russia, they had carbon-moderated piles. And the bad thing about carbon is it will burn. It gets on fire, and you can't put it out. So everything that we do in this country is with heavy water. That's used as the moderator.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Interviewer
sp.p: Now, what stadium are you -- when you say --

sp.speaker: Watson Warriner
sp.p: Okay. Get back to the stadium. This was in the Chicago stadium. And they were going to run the experiment there. And the reason they had it under the concrete stadium was if they had unfortunately -- an unfortunate accident. Let's say things went wrong and they had an explosion, that would help contain -- help contain the explosion. And the contamination of an area. So that's why it was under --

sp.speaker: Unidentified Interviewer
sp.p: Under the stadium?

sp.speaker: Watson Warriner
sp.p: -- under the concrete stadium.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Interviewer
sp.p: Okay. Now, did they use the same -- now, you said they used two different size bombs. Nagasaki and Hiroshima were two different size bombs, right?

sp.speaker: Watson Warriner
sp.p: They're two different bombs. The first bomb is a U-235 bomb.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Interviewer
sp.p: Would you call that Big Boy?

sp.speaker: Watson Warriner
sp.p: That was Little Boy.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Interviewer
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Watson Warriner
sp.p: And it came out of Oak Ridge. Oak Ridge did that. Oak Ridge, Tennessee. And the way they -- actually, Oak Ridge did not create anything. What they did, they had a massive ability to separate, do a physical separation of U-235 and U-238, which are the principal parts of uranium. And the part that is fissionable is U-235, which only turns out to be 7/10 of 1 percent of uranium. 99.3 percent of uranium is U-238, and that is not fissionable, so -- But they -- they were able through four different -- four processes, enormous processes, of doing this separation. And they did it. They accomplished that. And they --

sp.speaker: Unidentified Interviewer
sp.p: And that was the first bomb that they dropped --

sp.speaker: Watson Warriner
sp.p: That was the first bomb, containing U-235. And they called it -- you know, that was Little Boy. The way you fire that, you can -- what you have is you have two pieces of U-235, and you rammed them together. Basically it's like a rifle barrel.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Interviewer
sp.p: So it wasn't an impact bomb? It was a -- it was a -- it was detonated before it hit the ground?

sp.speaker: Watson Warriner
sp.p: Yeah. Well, they both were detonated before -- before they hit the ground. But that's what they did at Oak Ridge. Now, the thing of it is, as you recall, they're trying to get the .7 percent, less than 1 percent, the U-235, out of the uranium. Well, it's a big waste of uranium. You're not using 99 percent of it. Now, the way to really go, if it will work, is to take the U-two-thirty -- the U-238, which is at 99.7 percent of material, and convert it to plutonium, to plutonium. And that's what Enrico did under the stadium, and that's what DuPont did on a huge scale. So by the time -- I mean, it's unusual. It's a manmade element, 94 is. And so people say what about Element 93? Well, the 93 is created in the reactor. The reactor is a batch process. It takes several months to go from uranium -- the stuff is --

sp.speaker: Unidentified Interviewer
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Watson Warriner
sp.p: -- about two or three months. But it goes through nep -- I think it's neptunium is 93. And neptunium converts itself to 94. It's all done within the reactor. So -- so what this is -- what DuPont did was created this plutonium on a massive scale. By the end of 1945, DuPont -- a lot of people wondered did we have any more bombs to drop? The question is we had plenty more stuff. By the end of 1945, you know, first bombs were -- first ones were August the 6th. The plutonium bomb was dropped August the 9th. By the end of -- that was -- what? 1945. By the end of 1945, DuPont had produced well over 200 pounds of plutonium, which would be enough, as I remember, 19 Nagasaki bombs. So Truman had plenty more stuff to drop if nobody wanted to give up. So you might say today where do we stand with this? And I would think DuPont today would -- we've got tons and tons of plutonium.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Interviewer
sp.p: DuPont --

sp.speaker: Watson Warriner
sp.p: I would think it would be somewhere around -- just my personal guess; I don't know. It would be maybe 90 tons. That's a pure guess.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Interviewer
sp.p: Where are they keeping this? Or do you know? This --

sp.speaker: Watson Warriner
sp.p: I don't actually know where they keep it. But it's under -- it's -- it's under closely -- closely guarded secret.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Interviewer
sp.p: And DuPont has this?

sp.speaker: Watson Warriner
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Interviewer
sp.p: Oh, no, no, no. The government.

sp.speaker: Watson Warriner
sp.p: No. The government has it. As a matter of fact, if you -- what happened -- we're pretty much finished with the --

sp.speaker: Unidentified Interviewer
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Watson Warriner
sp.p: -- the -- the Hanford engineer works, so --

sp.speaker: Unidentified Interviewer
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah. We're --

sp.speaker: Watson Warriner
sp.p: But what happened, we thought the Russians, would take them 10 years to get that bomb, but they didn't. They exploded the bomb in 1949. In four years. So now what the hell's the United States going to do? The minute you have an atomic bomb, you can have a hydrogen weapon, a thermonuclear bomb, because the atomic bomb is a trigger to a thermonuclear weapon. So now the United States cannot sit idly by and let Russia, who now has an atomic bomb, begin to make thermonuclear weapons, which are the most fearsome weapons you've ever heard in your life. I mean, it destroys whole countries. And so what they did, what the government did, they had -- came to DuPont again, said, "Look. We've got to do it. You've got to help us out." So DuPont, right away, they started -- we started working 1950. The bomb went off in 1949. They dragged all of us back into this in 1950, and between 1950 and '55, we designed and built and started operation of the Savannah River plant in Aiken, South Carolina.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Interviewer
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Watson Warriner
sp.p: Yes. And now we -- at Aiken, we had five reactors. And these are heavy-water-moderated. So the plant -- one of the plants that we designed and built back in the early days of the war, as I began my lecture, the heavy water is now -- the initial heavy water is coming out of Wabash River ordnance works. That was one of the plants. But they had refined the process and had been able to make a much better product than they had back in -- when they first went up. And I saw it -- at the Hanford -- at the Savannah River plant, they put in probably what is the world's largest heavy water plant in the world. It's there. It must be about 144 big towers. It looked like a big oil -- oil refinery.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Interviewer
sp.p: Yeah, it does.

sp.speaker: Watson Warriner
sp.p: But that's where they're making the -- separating the heavy water from the regular water. And that will supply the five reactors and supply heavy water to many other places. So we had five reactors that were heavy-water- moderated, and we also had separations areas, separa -- so what we made there was the same -- what we made there; different process used in the -- the separations area, but we accomplished the same thing.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Interviewer
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Watson Warriner
sp.p: And we made not only plutonium there at the Savannah River plant, but we made tritium. Now, tritium is a material -- it's a gas. And that is used in thermonuclear weapons. We made tritium. And I'm quite sure the way you make tritium is that you take the metal lithium and irradiate lithium in a reactor, and you get a gas, radio -- and it's slightly radioactive. The problem with -- and you need the tritium to go along with hydrogen to make the weapons. And one of the problems with tritium is its half-life is only seven and a half years. So it disappears with age. You can't -- you can't speed it up, and you can't slow it down. The one thing about plutonium, its half-life is about twenty -- two thousand -- 20-some thousand years, so you don't have to worry about plutonium disappearing, but -- So what really happened, along about '55, in that period -- and I worked on that from start to finish, '55. And frankly, we had finished up the design and ended up there as being a senior design engineer, and they had given me the job to handle all the waste. And the first thing you're going to do now is to start concentrating that waste, and we were in negotiating with France because France was pioneering glassifying this waste. And that was when I decided I had seen enough of engineering, and I had an opportunity to go into marketing, which I did, at the blessing of Granville M. Read. And so for the next 27, 26 years, I was in the plastics department in marketing. But let's go back to -- now to the Savannah River plant. Along about this period, between '55 and '60, Khrushchev was a very dominant person. He would come to the UN and take his shoe off and bang it and make fun of the United States, "What a small country you have, and we are many, many times bigger than you are. And look at the -- at the terrible little bitty satellites you're shooting up; nothing but the size of grapefruit. And you can see our big satellites. You could see those with the naked eye." So now, in '62, he decides, well, we'll put missiles into Cuba. And he started that. Well, by this time, the United States had produced thermonuclear weapons, and we had deployed these in submarines and airplanes. And we had also, I'm sure, made it very well-known to the Russian people that run everything what we had. I mean, we didn't try to hide it anymore. We wanted them to know. Because we had the facility for destroying the whole goddamn country about 10 times over.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Interviewer
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Watson Warriner
sp.p: And so somebody -- finally Khrushchev began to understand this. And that's when he got to remove the missile. We came very, very close to having a problem. 1962, when he removed the missiles from Cuba, and that was the beginning of the end of the Russian nation. And it was all done by the United States of America. Us. Europeans didn't have a damn thing to do with it. We love them. They're good friends of ours, but they all thank us for what we did.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Interviewer
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Watson Warriner
sp.p: We're the ones that brought the Russians to their knees. We stood them down thermonuclear, in a nuclear way, and we broke them financially, to the point where they realized that their system was not productive. They con -- they convinced themselves that what they were -- what they were doing was not right. And not morally right; it was just nonproductive.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Interviewer
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Watson Warriner
sp.p: And so --

sp.speaker: Unidentified Interviewer
sp.p: How are we doing? All right? We good?

sp.speaker: Unidentified Speaker
sp.p: Mm-hmm. Let me check tape.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Interviewer
sp.p: You want to check tape? I think it was good.

sp.speaker: Watson Warriner
sp.p: Was I -- (Conclusion of interview.)
